repos.title: How Far Can You Steer? Behavior-Capability Frontiers in Contrastive Activation Addition
repos.paper_summary: This paper treats activation steering with Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) as a constrained selection problem. For each behavior, it chooses the steering coefficient that maximizes behavioral gain while accuracy loss on MMLU, ARC-Challenge, and HellaSwag stays within a budget of 1, 3, or 5 absolute percentage points. The layer is fixed from behavioral validation data, and the operating point is frozen before held-out evaluation. Experiments cover four 7–8B instruction-tuned models and seven behaviors. Validation-selected behavioral gains predict held-out gains with a Spearman correlation of 0.945. Among nonzero operating points, joint held-out survival (behavioral support plus passing all protected benchmarks) is 37.5% at the 1% budget, 72.7% at 3%, and 76.8% at 5%. Norm-matched, label-shuffled, and KL-matched random directions produce weaker effects than CAA, so the effects depend on learned directions. Cosine geometry is only modestly predictive of cross-behavior causal transfer. Points that pass the protected benchmarks can still degrade GSM8K or WikiText-2 and transfer unevenly to TruthfulQA and open-ended generation. Limitations: only 7–8B models and CAA were tested, behavioral evaluation uses binary choices, the LLM judge was not validated against human annotations, and the 1% results may reflect conservative confidence bounds.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Steering should be treated as a constrained selection problem with explicit capability-loss budgets, not judged on behavior alone.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior steering methods change strength or space, while this paper keeps CAA fixed and studies how to select its operating range.

digest_headlines.heading: Behavior–Capability Frontiers
digest_headlines.headline: The frontier picks, at a layer fixed on validation data, the coefficient with the largest behavior gain that meets a capability bound.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Four instruction-tuned models, seven behaviors, and three protected benchmarks share one protocol with fixed splits.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Capability-constrained steering survives held-out testing for 72.7% of nonzero points at a 3% budget but only 37.5% at 1%.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Under tight budgets, capability preservation rather than behavioral effect limits steering, and frontier claims hold only for the evaluated suite.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The usable steering range depends on the allowed capability loss, model, behavior, layer, and direction, not on one coefficient.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover four 7–8B models and binary-choice core tests, with an unvalidated model judge and a strict 1% budget sensitive to sampling.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Steering is dual use, and passing capability constraints does not establish deployment safety.

digest_headlines.heading: Use of Generative AI
digest_headlines.headline: Generative AI assistants supported scripting, debugging, visualization, and manuscript polishing, and one model served as a blinded judge.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers behavioral data and prompting, layer diagnostics, frontier and holdout results, specificity controls, geometry, open-ended details, compute, and reproducibility.

repos.title: Prior-data fitted networks for variable selection
repos.paper_summary: This paper presents CD-PFN and PC-PFN, two prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) that estimate posterior inclusion probabilities (PIPs) for Bayesian variable selection. CD-PFN targets conditional dependence of each covariate on the response, and PC-PFN targets parent or child status in a causal DAG. Both are transformers trained on simulated datasets from a prior, so they return PIPs in one forward pass without posterior samples or dataset-specific modeling. On 50 semi-synthetic TCGA trials (n=100, p=50, five true covariates), CD-PFN's AUPRC is 0.93 on linear responses (spike-and-slab 0.95), 0.89 on in-prior nonlinear responses (BKMR 0.72), and 0.58 on held-out nonlinear responses (BKMR 0.41). CD-PFN takes 0.2 seconds per dataset on a CPU, versus 243 seconds for TabPFN with permutation importance. On a linear g-prior with exact PIPs, mean absolute error falls from 0.19 to 0.03 after two hours of fine-tuning. Limitations: FDR control is approximate because the PIPs are approximate, and PC-PFN's parent and child probabilities depend on the prior when the data cannot distinguish models.

digest_headlines.heading: 1. Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: CD-PFN performs best in both nonlinear simulated settings and nearly matches linear spike-and-slab on linear responses, without tuning.

digest_headlines.heading: 2. PFNs for variable selection
digest_headlines.headline: Training with binary cross-entropy on simulated data targets the posterior probability itself, so no posterior sampling is needed.

digest_headlines.heading: 3. Priors
digest_headlines.headline: The priors mix an X-first class with structural causal models, covering covariates that are effects of the response or share latent causes with it.

digest_headlines.heading: 4. Simulation studies
digest_headlines.headline: Across simulations, CD-PFN ranks covariates best in all 30 settings and PC-PFN ranks parents and children best in all nine gene expression settings.

digest_headlines.heading: 5. Real data
digest_headlines.headline: CD-PFN selects 15 of 18 established biomarkers in multi-biomarker tasks, and PC-PFN orients all 45 demographic selections correctly.

digest_headlines.heading: 6. Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors propose studying how priors shape performance, adapting networks to new priors, and extending the framework to other binary targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Code and data availability
digest_headlines.headline: The varselpfn package, trained networks, and reproduction code are publicly available, and all datasets come from public sources.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists related methods, setup and architecture details, prior construction, and real-data specifics for the biomarker, survey, and light tunnel studies.

repos.title: FLINT: Coupling Proximal Initialization and Bounded Stochasticity for Flow-Matching Inverse Problems
repos.paper_summary: FLINT is a training-free, two-stage sampler for flow-matching inverse problems that pairs a short source-space optimization of the initial noise with guided sampling under a bounded stochasticity schedule. Stage 1 optimizes the initial noise $\bm{\mu}_\phi$ for a few iterations on a variational objective combining data fidelity, a KL term to a Gaussian prior, and a cumulant regularizer that penalizes non-Gaussian drift. Stage 2 runs guided flow sampling from this initialization while limiting the cumulative injected noise $G=\int_0^1 g_t^2\,dt$. The authors derive a terminal stability bound on the mean-square deviation from a reference trajectory, which scales with the initialization error $\delta^2$ and with $d\cdot G$, under one-sided Lipschitz assumptions on the posterior velocity and score. On Gaussian deblurring with FFHQ, they report a sufficiency regime up to perturbation scale $C_0\approx 0.4$, beyond which reconstruction quality degrades, and show that larger $G$ erodes the benefit of the initialization. The paper reports strong perceptual quality and competitive distortion across inverse problems. Stated limitations include inherited biases of the pretrained generator and reduced quality on structurally complex scenes with many objects.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing posterior samplers either fix the starting noise or optimize it alone; FLINT couples both choices.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Background defines flow-based posterior sampling and the truncated, shortcut-based gradients that make source optimization cheaper.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis: Coupling of Proximal Initialization and Sampling Stochasticity
digest_headlines.headline: The stability bound predicts a sufficiency regime and erosion by stochasticity, and Gaussian deblurring experiments are consistent with both.

digest_headlines.heading: Method: The FLINT Framework
digest_headlines.headline: FLINT runs a few proximal optimization steps for initialization, then guided sampling under a bell-shaped stochasticity schedule.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: FLINT outperforms flow matching baselines, and ablations show that proximal initialization and the bell-shaped schedule both contribute.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion restates the coupling principle, and the limitations are inherited prior biases and weaker results on complex scenes.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists energy-bound proofs, cumulant and initialization comparisons, excessive optimization, posterior variance, and extra qualitative results.

repos.title: Chronos: Sequential Identity-Preserving Video Generation by Temporal Anchoring
repos.paper_summary: Chronos is a training-free framework for identity-preserving video generation that handles single-subject facial identity preservation (Track 1) and multi-segment sequential actions with several subjects (Track 2). Semantic Prompt Anchoring uses a GPT model to extract identity cues from reference images and conservatively rewrite the prompt. Visual Frame Anchoring uses an image-to-image model to produce a first-frame anchor, or a cascade of keyframe anchors for sequential captions. Metric-Guided Candidate Routing generates candidates from Wan2.2 I2V-14B, Seedance, and Wan FLF2V, then selects the highest weighted score across text alignment, identity, subject, motion, quality, and LLM-based dimensions. A selected video goes to human review if any critical metric falls below a threshold. On Track 1, Chronos scores 0.6769 Total Score versus 0.6214 for RefAlign-14B, about 9.0% higher. On Track 2, it scores 0.6102 versus 0.5725 for Phantom-14B, a 6.6% gain. The paper reports first place in both tracks of the ACM MM 2026 IPVG challenge. Ablations use the first 100 cases, and the paper states the trends match the full set. Limitations: the pipeline depends on proprietary GPT and Seedance models, and the Track 1 identity score for Chronos (0.6840) is below RefAlign's 0.7996.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Chronos is a training-free framework that unifies single-segment identity preservation with multi-segment sequential action generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior identity-preserving methods often trade identity fidelity against motion, and multi-subject methods still struggle with temporal consistency.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Chronos selects the top-scoring candidate from several generators and sends critical-failure outputs to human review.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Adding all components raises Total Score over the baseline on both tracks, from 0.6353 to 0.6833 and 0.5803 to 0.6530.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Chronos is summarized as a training-free framework whose selection step produced first place on both challenge tracks.

repos.title: When Is One Query per Template Enough? Adapting Learned Cost Models to New Hardware
repos.paper_summary: This paper studies how to adapt a learned PostgreSQL runtime model to new hardware using runtimes of k queries measured on the new machine. Its primary method, the template correction, fits separate lines for serial and parallel plans and adds an offset for each measured query template. The authors timed the same plans of 1,162 TPC-H and TPC-DS queries in six environments. With one measured query per template, the correction reaches a geometric-mean median Q-error over templates of 1.10 on TPC-H and 1.19 on TPC-DS, close to the same correction applied to a model trained on the new machine. Fine-tuning a DACE-style neural model gains at most 2%. For templates with no measured query, no tested correction is more than 2% better than a single speed factor. On TPC-H at scale factor 10, the errors follow these results, but two of five repeated tests miss. On the Join Order Benchmark, the forest model errs by 2.36 even when retrained, and no correction gains much. Limitations: one database system, two virtualized x86 machines, and no data larger than memory.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: A runtime model moved to new hardware can be corrected from a few measured queries; this paper asks which, and how many.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem and Background
digest_headlines.headline: A query's slowdown on new hardware is its own factor, so corrections need runtimes measured there, and template share measures how much a constant explains.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods Compared
digest_headlines.headline: Six corrections and six selection strategies are compared against refitting, a neural fine-tune, and an oracle reference.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Identical plans were timed in six environments on TPC-H and TPC-DS, with corrections scored on held-out test queries.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: No single factor describes the slowdown: 0.69 to 0.94 of its variance lies between templates.

digest_headlines.heading: Lessons
digest_headlines.headline: Measure one query per template, chosen round robin, and do not expect corrections to help on templates never measured.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier work moves cost models with retraining, fine-tuning, model shift or per-template calibration; this paper adds a controlled measurement.

digest_headlines.heading: Threats to Validity
digest_headlines.headline: The study covers one database system, two virtualized machines and data that fit in memory.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: In these environments one measured query per template brought the moved model within 3% of the same correction on a retrained model.

repos.title: A low-rank decoder bottleneck bounds reliability in foundation-model perturbation prediction
repos.paper_summary:
The paper audits the state-transition (ST) decoder of STATE, paired with three encoders (SE-600M, scGPT, Tahoe-x1) across four CRISPRi cell lines, and proposes predicted-NN-distance as a per-prediction confidence score. The decoder's first attention layer has a low-rank output: projecting it onto 44–3232 directions fixed from training activations preserves mean per-perturbation Pearson delta correlation (PDC). PDC declines as the cosine distance from a perturbation's observed response to its nearest training response grows. Predicted-NN-distance computes that distance from the predicted response; its mean absolute Spearman correlation with PDC is 0.81, against 0.88 for the observed response. A threshold calibrated on other encoder–cell configurations transfers to held-out ones and remains predictive for drug perturbations.

Limitations: in Tahoe++ST part of the signal bypasses the first attention layer; the score is weaker when a whole gene family is absent from training; the Learn-then-Test guarantee fails when deployment perturbations lie farther from training than calibration perturbations; MLP layers were not intervened on, and the biological meaning of the directions is not established.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Perturbation predictions lose accuracy as their responses move away from training responses, so each prediction needs a reliability score.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Recent encoder-decoder predictors match linear baselines, and the authors open the decoder's first attention layer to find why.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: The methods project the first attention output onto top singular or fixed training directions and score each prediction by predicted-NN-distance.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Decoder accuracy falls far from training, and its first attention layer passes perturbation signal through a few fixed directions.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Benchmark scores mostly reflect how many test perturbations lie near training, and a threshold on the score transfers to held-out cell lines.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The acknowledgments credit two grant awards and declare no competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists configurations and hyperparameters, probe settings, intervention and threshold details, per-cell-line results, gene-family analyses, and related work.

repos.title: Time-to-Goal: Learned Temporal Metrics for Long-Horizon Planning with JEPA World Models
repos.paper_summary: Time-to-Goal (T2G) is a small learned temporal metric that replaces the Euclidean goal cost of flat LeWM, a JEPA world model, during planning. The encoder and predictor stay frozen. The authors argue that Euclidean goal costs weakly separate states at long temporal offsets, because the cross-covariance term changes less at larger offsets while the squared-mean and variance terms vary little. T2G is an MLP embedding with a learned scale, trained with a margin ranking loss on anchor, near, and far latents from offline trajectories. It uses only temporal order, with no rewards or policy labels, and adds 0.182M parameters, 1.6% of flat LeWM. Across four simulated benchmarks, averaged over three seeds with 50 tasks each, the last-n T2G cost raises mean planning success from 32.7% to 63.0%. Two-, three-, and four-level H-JEPA reach 53.3%, 61.7%, and 49.8%. The dense full-rollout variant is inconsistent and reaches 4.0% on Cube. The evidence is simulation only, and the paper does not test physical robots.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Flat JEPA planners with Euclidean goal costs give unreliable progress signals over long horizons, motivating a better cost alone.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Euclidean contrast shrinks at long offsets, so T2G learns a margin-ranked distance over latent triples from offline trajectories.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: T2G last-n raises the four-benchmark average success rate from 32.7% to 63.0%, near or above hierarchical baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Related work separates T2G from hierarchical JEPA planners and from reward-based temporal learning methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The goal cost strongly affects latent planning, and trajectory order can supply supervision that shapes it.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists hardware, the triple sampling procedure, training hyperparameters, and per-environment input and sampling settings.

repos.title: OdorSpaces: Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation in 3D Environments
repos.paper_summary:
OdorSpaces is a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation, in which an agent uses egocentric depth images, gas-density measurements, and pose history to reach an invisible odor source. It augments Habitat-Sim, with scenes from Replica and Matterport3D, by sampling odor fields that Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) computes in 3D. Two scenarios are defined: propane gas leak and methanol pool fire, where CO2 density stands in as the fire odor. The paper also provides a reference policy: a PPO-trained agent with modality-specific encoders, a fused recurrent memory, and a distance-based reward with a gas-gradient bonus. Training uses a curriculum that raises the initial geodesic distance from 1.5 m to 9.0 m over 30M steps.

On propane, the policy reaches 65.26% SPL on Replica (final distance 1.48 m) and 63.82% on Matterport3D (1.59 m). The strongest baseline, Dual-Recurrent Threshold RL, gets 54.50% and 65.41% SPL. On methanol, the policy reaches 24.72% SPL on Replica and 14.16% on Matterport3D, while rule-based baselines reach 0.00% SPL. Results are over three test seeds. The odor sensor is idealized, odor fields are precomputed, and the benchmark starts after detection rather than covering full plume finding.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: OdorSpaces provides a physics-based benchmark for navigating toward odor sources using vision and gas sensing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Machine olfaction work mainly addresses semantic odor perception, and source localization methods often use simplified plumes.

digest_headlines.heading: OdorSpaces: A Benchmark for Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation
digest_headlines.headline: Agents must reach a hidden odor source within a fixed time budget, using precomputed FDS gas fields in Habitat-Sim scenes.

digest_headlines.heading: Visual-Olfactory Navigation Policy
digest_headlines.headline: A recurrent policy fuses visual, olfactory and pose features and trains with proximal policy optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: The policy has the top mean success-weighted path length in three of four settings; the only exception is Matterport3D propane.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper frames OdorSpaces as a first benchmark for this task and lists precomputed fields and idealized sensing as limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers FDS settings, scene processing, sensor layout, baseline details, extra ablations, and spawn-distance generalization.

repos.title: Mitigating Spurious Invariance in Contrastive Learning: A Probabilistic Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Medical Image Analysis
repos.paper_summary: The paper proposes probabilistic contrastive learning (ProbCL), a self-supervised method that maps each volumetric medical image to a Gaussian distribution over embeddings rather than a fixed vector, and a unified framework that combines it with other SSL objectives. The backbone is the SwinUNETR encoder. For two augmented views, a symmetric KL divergence between their Gaussians (the DCL loss) has a closed form in which each latent dimension is weighted by its inverse variances. A SimSiam-style sample-wise loss (SCL), computed on reparameterized samples with a stop-gradient, prevents collapse, and a KL-to-prior term keeps the variances from degenerating. The total loss is a weighted sum of these three terms. The theoretical section shows that, under a locally linear signal-noise model, the DCL mean term upper-bounds a precision-weighted least-squares objective. The provided text ends before the calibration condition that the analysis requires. The abstract claims better results than SSL baselines on medical segmentation and classification, with robustness, label-efficiency, and compute analyses, but the excerpt contains no experimental numbers.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Contrastive learning enforces invariance that may suppress subtle medical features, motivating a probabilistic embedding framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior SSL work covers predictive, generative and contrastive methods, but spurious invariance in medical contrastive learning is rarely studied.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each image becomes a Gaussian embedding aligned by a symmetric Kullback-Leibler loss, with predictive and generative heads added.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments on four downstream tasks, pre-trained on 1,589 unlabeled CT scans, compare the method against supervised, general and medical SSL baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion reports outperforming baselines, while naming Gaussian, diagonal-covariance and small-pretraining limits.

repos.title: Toward an Optimal Configuration for Tree Species Classification from Bark Images: A Leakage-Safe Ablation Study
repos.paper_summary: This paper ablates the main design choices for bark-based tree species classification on the public BarkNet 1.0 dataset (20 species). It uses a tree-level split to prevent same-trunk leakage and five-fold cross-validation with ConvNeXt-V2 backbones. The factors varied one at a time are patch size (160 to 512 px), aggregation rule, single- versus two-stage training, backbone size (pico, nano, tiny), whole-image baseline, and number of test-time patches. Attention-based multiple instance learning is compared with majority voting. Per-patch accuracy rises from 75.6% at 160 px to 89.6% at 512 px, and image-level accuracy plateaus near 94.9% around 512 px. Attention pooling exceeds majority voting by at most 0.7 percentage points. Backbone capacity changes accuracy by less than one point, two-stage training gives no advantage, and whole-image classification reaches 91.9%. Accuracy saturates at about 64 patches. Limitations: a single dataset and region, class imbalance, hyperparameters tuned only for the nano backbone at 224 px, and training and evaluation bags of different sizes.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Bark identification is practical, but design choices for tile-based deep learning have not been compared jointly, and image-level splits can leak.

digest_headlines.heading: Materials and Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Tree-level five-fold tests on BarkNet 1.0 vary patch size, aggregation, training, backbone capacity and bag size, with eight hypotheses.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Image-level accuracy plateaus near 94.9% at 512 px, and learned aggregation beats voting by at most 0.73 pp.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Recommended setup is patches around 512 px with a nano backbone; aggregation and training matter less.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: Patch size dominates accuracy, so the study recommends the largest patches that still leave enough to average over, with a nano backbone.

digest_headlines.heading: Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The research received no external funding, and its experiments ran on Digital Research Alliance of Canada infrastructure.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and Code Availability
digest_headlines.headline: The BarkNet 1.0 dataset and reproduction code, including fold assignments, are published in two GitHub repositories.

digest_headlines.heading: Conflicts of Interest
digest_headlines.headline: The author declares no conflict of interest.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of Generative AI Use
digest_headlines.headline: The author reports using Anthropic Claude only for editing and LaTeX formatting, and takes full responsibility for the content.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists exact per-patch, aggregation, bag-size and per-class values behind the main figures and tables.
